headings.text: CNPG and the seven database clusters

blocks.html:
⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page maps where the platform's state actually lives: the seven CloudNativePG database clusters, the persistent volumes (including the one whose loss invalidates every issued token), and the secret model — everything generated in-cluster by External Secrets Operator, shared across namespaces with a small RBAC pattern, and, at this stage, backed up by nothing at all. Read it if you develop against the platform or are deciding whether to trust it with data.

CNPG and the seven database clusters

All relational storage is managed by the CloudNativePG operator (cnpg-1.27.1, installed in infra-phase1, running in the cnpg-system namespace). Each service that needs Postgres declares its own Cluster custom resource in its own namespace; the operator turns that CR into a Postgres pod, a PVC, Services, and generated credentials. There is no shared database server — the seven clusters are seven isolated single-purpose Postgres instances:

Cluster Namespace Image Storage Consumer
rmapi-postgres opendefence-system operator default (postgresql:18.0-system-trixie) 5Gi rmapi
keycloak-postgres opendefence-system operator default (postgresql:18.0-system-trixie) 5Gi keycloak
tak-postgres app-tak postgis:15-3.4 (PostGIS) 5Gi takinit → TAK services
mtx-postgres app-mtx postgresql:18.3 1Gi mtxrmapi
matrix-postgres app-matrix postgresql:18.0-system-trixie 5Gi synapse-server
mas-postgres app-matrix postgresql:18.0-system-trixie 1Gi mas
battlelog-postgres app-battlelog postgis:18-3.6-system-trixie (PostGIS) 5Gi battlelog

Every cluster is instances: 1. There is no high availability anywhere in the database estate — no replicas, no failover. If a database pod's node goes down, that service is down, and because storage is node-local (see below), the replacement pod can only run where the volume lives — if the node is gone for good, so is the data.

A few clusters carry extra shape. tak-postgres and battlelog-postgres are PostGIS images with a CNPG Database CR enabling postgis, postgis_topology, fuzzystrmatch and postgis_tiger_geocoder; tak-postgres additionally runs postInitApplicationSQL copied from the legacy stack's pg_init/03_tak.sh and pins its image to postgis:15-3.4 (a newer postgis:18-3.6-system-trixie line sits commented out in the manifest). rmapi-postgres and keycloak-postgres set no imageName and get the operator's default image — which is why the Zarf build has to append ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql:18.0-system-trixie manually (zarf dev find-images can't see an image that appears in no manifest).

Credentials are never written by hand. For each cluster, CNPG generates a <cluster>-app Secret (keys host, dbname, username, password, uri), and the consuming Deployment pulls what it needs via valueFrom.secretKeyRef — e.g. rmapi reads rmapi-postgres-app, mas reads mas-postgres-app. The diagram below shows the whole estate; dotted lines are the operator reconciling Cluster CRs across namespaces, solid arrows are apps consuming the generated -app credentials Secret.

blocks.html:
Persistent volumes

Beyond the volumes CNPG provisions for its own clusters (the Storage column above), the platform declares these PVCs explicitly:

PVC Namespace Size Mounted by Holds
rmapi-data opendefence-system 100Mi rmapi JWT signing keypair (JWT_PRIVKEY_PATH=/data/persistent/private/rm_jwtsign.key)
openldap-data opendefence-system 1Gi openldap LDAP directory data
tak-data app-tak 5Gi TAK server containers TAK Server data and configuration
ca-public app-tak 1Gi TAK server containers Split CA certificates (root_ca.pem / intermediate_ca.pem)
le-certs app-tak 1Gi TAK server containers Let's Encrypt certificates
shared-tak app-tak 1Gi TAK server containers Shared TAK configuration/data
takrmapi-data app-tak 1Gi takrmapi TAK integration API state
mtx-data app-mtx 1Gi MediaMTX containers MediaMTX server data
matrix-data app-matrix 1Gi matrixrmapi Matrix integration API state
synapse-server-data app-matrix 5Gi synapse-server Synapse data directory (/data)
mas-data app-matrix 1Gi mas Matrix Authentication Service state
battlelog-data app-battlelog 5Gi battlelog Battlelog application data

One more volume exists outside this table: the Loki Helm chart in the monitoring namespace claims a 10Gi volume for log storage (filesystem backend, 30-day retention) — covered in Observability pipeline.

rmapi-data deserves the emphasis. It is the smallest volume on the list and the most consequential: rmapi signs the JWTs used across the platform with the private key at /data/persistent/private/rm_jwtsign.key on this volume (the key's passphrase, JWT_PRIVKEY_PASS, comes from the generated rmapi-runtime-secrets Secret). Lose this 100Mi PVC and rmapi will generate a fresh keypair — every previously issued token stops validating, and everything that holds one has to re-authenticate.

Storage classes are deliberately unremarkable: no manifest sets a storageClassName except one — the cloud overlay of opendefence-system pins openldap-data to local-path. Everything else uses the cluster default, which is standard on kind (local) and local-path on k3s (cloud). Either way, all data is node-local: a PVC is a directory on the node that first scheduled the pod. There is no networked or replicated storage layer.

Secrets without a vault

Every secret in the platform that CNPG doesn't generate is generated by the External Secrets Operator, in-cluster, at first apply. Each component that needs a secret declares a Password generator (generators.external-secrets.io/v1alpha1) plus an ExternalSecret whose dataFrom.sourceRef.generatorRef points at it; ESO rolls the random value and writes the target Secret. Three generator shapes recur:

  • password-32-8digits-no-symbols — 32 chars, 8 digits, no symbols; the workhorse used by almost everything
  • password-64-alphanumeric — 64-char alphanumeric, used by the Matrix stack's high-entropy secrets
  • password-32-hex — 32-char, hex-encoded, used only for MAS_ENCRYPTION_SECRET

Nearly all ExternalSecrets set refreshInterval: "0" — generate once, then leave the value alone. The notable generated secrets:

Secret Namespace What it carries
keycloak-init-user opendefence-system Keycloak admin credentials (KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD etc.), used by keycloak, the keycloak-init Job and rmapi
keycloak-ldap-admin opendefence-system OpenLDAP admin bind credentials (LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD)
rmapi-runtime-secrets opendefence-system JWT_PRIVKEY_PASS — passphrase for the JWT signing key on rmapi-data
callsign-validity-shared-secret opendefence-system Shared secret between the Traefik callsign plugin and rmapi's internal check endpoint
tak-secrets app-tak takserver-cert-pass + tak-ca-pass (generated) and ldap-admin-password (copied — see next section)
mtx-secrets app-mtx API_PASSWORD, SRT_PUB_PASSWORD, SRT_READ_PASSWORD — MediaMTX credentials, consumed by mtxrmapi via envFrom with prefix RMMTX_
matrix-secrets app-matrix SYNAPSE_MACAROON_SECRET_KEY, MAS_SYNAPSE_SECRET, MAS_ADMIN_CLIENT_SECRET, MAS_ENCRYPTION_SECRET, LIVEKIT_API_SECRET
grafana-admin-password monitoring Grafana admin password

There is no external secret backend: no Vault, no sealed-secrets, no SOPS-encrypted files in git. This is a property of the design, not an oversight waiting for configuration — the repo contains zero secret material, so there is nothing to leak from source control and no decryption key to manage at deploy time. The flip side is that the only copy of every credential lives inside the cluster (in the Secrets ESO and CNPG wrote). Tear the cluster down and every password, shared secret and passphrase is gone with it; a redeploy generates a fresh, unrelated set. The birth of a typical secret looks like this:

blocks.html:
The cross-namespace sharing pattern

Kubernetes Secrets are namespaced, and sometimes a value born in one namespace is needed in another. The platform solves this with ESO's Kubernetes provider rather than duplicating generators (which would produce two different passwords). The recipe, used identically in both places it appears:

  1. The source Secret lives in namespace A (both current instances: opendefence-system), with a Role/RoleBinding in A granting get/list/watch on secrets to a foreign ServiceAccount.
  2. A dedicated reader ServiceAccount exists in consumer namespace B — one SA per sharing relationship, so the grant is as narrow as possible.
  3. A **SecretStore** in B uses provider.kubernetes with remoteNamespace: opendefence-system, authenticating as that ServiceAccount.
  4. An **ExternalSecret** in B reads the remote key through the store and writes a local copy (optionally merging it with locally generated values).

Generalized, with both concrete instances labeled on each node:

get list watch on secrets"] end subgraph nsb["Consumer namespace - app-tak / traefik-system"] sa["Reader ServiceAccount
tak-ldap-secret-reader / callsign-secret-reader"] store["SecretStore - provider kubernetes
tak-keycloak-secrets / callsign-validity-source"] es["ExternalSecret
tak-secrets / callsign-validity-shared-secret"] dst["Local copy Secret
tak-secrets / callsign-validity-shared-secret"] end rbac -.->|"authorizes"| sa store -->|"authenticates as"| sa store -->|"reads"| src es -->|"via"| store es -->|"writes"| dst

blocks.html:
The two instances:

  • LDAP bind credentials into **app-tak**. TAK Server authenticates users against OpenLDAP, so it needs the same admin bind password Keycloak's LDAP federation uses. The tak-secrets ExternalSecret (SA tak-ldap-secret-reader, SecretStore tak-keycloak-secrets) copies LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD out of keycloak-ldap-admin and merges it with two freshly generated keystore passwords (takserver-cert-pass, tak-ca-pass) into a single Secret the TAK first-run script consumes.
  • Callsign shared secret into **traefik-system**. The shared kustomize component k8s/_shared/traefik-secret-mirror (applied in infra-phase2) mirrors callsign-validity-shared-secret from opendefence-system into traefik-system via SA callsign-secret-reader and SecretStore callsign-validity-source, with refreshInterval: "20s" — the one ExternalSecret that keeps re-syncing, so Traefik and rmapi converge on the same value even though the source Secret is only created phases later. Traefik consumes the mirror as env RM_CALLSIGN_VALIDITY_SECRET (optional: false). What the plugin does with it is covered in Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

Backups: none configured

Stated plainly: the platform takes no backups of anything. No CNPG backup sections, no Barman or object-store integration, no WAL archiving, no VolumeSnapshot machinery, no scheduled dumps. Combined with instances: 1 everywhere and node-local storage on both kind and k3s, the failure math is unforgiving:

  • Lose a node (or its disk) and you lose every database and PVC that lived on it, permanently.
  • Lose rmapi-data and every issued JWT is invalidated (new signing key on next start).
  • Lose rmapi-postgres and enrollment state — users, callsigns, product ownership — is gone.
  • Lose the cluster entirely and the CA secrets go with it (they live in etcd, not on PVs), orphaning every client certificate ever issued.

For the closed alpha this is a documented trade-off, not a hidden one: deployments are treated as rebuildable, and task up / the Zarf package can stand a fresh instance up from nothing. But a rebuilt instance is a new instance — new CA, new secrets, new empty databases — and everyone re-enrolls. If you are running anything you would mind losing, the operational workarounds (and what teardown actually destroys) are covered in Day-2 operations (Kubernetes) and Troubleshooting & teardown.
